transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you for fitting me in. It’s, uh... it's a little hard to pin down exactly, because I’m not in any pain or anything like that. I've been working in IT management for a long time now—managing computer systems, dealing with servers and networks, that sort of thing—so I’m pretty used to troubleshooting when something isn't working right. You look for the root cause. But mostly, I came in today because I’m just... I'm tired in a way that really doesn’t make any logical sense to me. 

I mean, I’m getting my sleep. I go to bed at a reasonable hour, I sleep through the night, I haven't changed my routine or my mattress or anything at all. And I can still keep up at work, I’m still doing my job and getting everything done that I need to do with my team, but... well, it just feels like I’m running on a completely low battery before the day even gets going. You know when a laptop says it's plugged in all night, but the charge just isn't holding, and the minute you open it up in the morning, it's already dying? That’s exactly how I feel. I wake up and I'm already drained, and I just drag that heavy feeling with me through the morning, into the office, through all my meetings... I just can't seem to figure out why I'm so wiped out when I'm doing everything I'm supposed to be doing to stay rested. I even tried adjusting my caffeine intake, thinking maybe that was throwing off my sleep cycles, but it hasn't made a lick of difference. It's just this constant exhaustion.
Have you noticed any decrease in interest in the things you usually enjoy doing?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because my wife was just saying something similar the other day. She noticed I haven't been out to the garage as much to get my gear ready for the weekend. I used to love fishing—have for years. I've got this little spot down by the lake, usually head out there early Saturday mornings. It used to be the highlight of my week, just the quiet, you know? And the garden, too. I've always taken pride in my tomatoes. I've got these Big Boys and some heirlooms I started from seed back in March, and usually I'm out there every evening, checking for hornworms, making sure the soil is just right. 

But lately... I don't know, for a long time now, actually, there's just been this... this sort of gray, flat feeling hanging over me most days. It's like the color has been drained out of everything. Even things I used to really look forward to, like going out on the boat, or tending to the garden, or even those Sunday evening concerts at the church that we've been going to for a decade... they just don't hold the same appeal. It's not that I actively dislike them now, it's just that they feel more like items on a checklist. Like, 'Okay, I need to water the tomatoes now,' or 'I suppose I should go sit in the pew and listen to the choir.' I do them because I'm supposed to, or because it's part of the routine, but that spark of enjoyment, that feeling of actually looking forward to it... it's just not there. It's all just so... flat. I keep thinking maybe if I just force myself to go through the motions, the enjoyment will come back, but it's like trying to start an engine with no spark plug. I just don't get it.
Do you often feel guilty or blame yourself for things?

Guilty? Blaming myself? Well... I mean, not really. Not any more than the average person, I suppose. I don't sit around beating myself up over things, if that's what you mean. 

I mean, sure, in my line of work—managing IT systems—if a server goes down or a network patch fails and knocks a whole department offline for an hour, yeah, I take responsibility. That's just part of being a manager. You have to own the mistakes your team makes, figure out where the breakdown in communication was, and fix the process. So in that sense, I'll say, "Okay, that's on me, I should have double-checked the backup protocol before we ran the update." But that's just professional accountability, you know? It's not this deep, lingering guilt that keeps me up at night. 

And at home... well, I guess sometimes I feel a little bad that my wife is noticing how flat I've been. Like I mentioned with the fishing and the gardening... I know she worries when I'm not out in the garage puttering around. I feel a twinge of guilt that I'm not being the most engaging company lately. Last week, she made my favorite pot roast—the one with the little pearl onions and the carrots that get all caramelized—and I just sat there chewing it, not really tasting it, and I could see her looking at me, waiting for me to say how good it was. I did say it was good, of course, but she knows me too well. She could tell my heart wasn't in it. I felt bad about that, because she put the effort in, but it's not like I'm walking around all day punishing myself for it. It's more just a passing thought of, "Well, I wish I could be a bit more lively for her sake." But no, I wouldn't say I'm plagued by guilt or constantly blaming myself for things going wrong in the world. I'm just... tired and flat, like I said.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, let me think back on that... you know, time sort of blurs together when every day feels like you're just wading through molasses, but if I really trace it back to when this heavy, flat feeling started to settle in and just... stay... it's been quite a while. 

I'd say it really began right around the time I got pulled back into full operational leadership at the company. That was... gosh, it was right after the big merger we had, when they consolidated the regional IT departments. So that would make it about two years and four months ago, give or take a couple of weeks. 

See, before that, I had sort of transitioned into more of an advisory role. I was still managing, but I had a couple of really sharp junior managers handling the day-to-day fires—the server crashes, the frantic calls from accounting about the payroll software—and I was focusing more on long-term strategy, infrastructure planning, you know, the big picture stuff. It was a good pace. I liked it. But then the merger happened, and one of those junior managers left for a startup, and the other one got transferred to the new corporate headquarters out of state. 

Suddenly, I was right back in the trenches. Full operational leadership. I'm talking about being the primary point of contact for every single network outage, every security patch that didn't deploy correctly, every complaint from the executive team about the Wi-Fi being slow in the boardroom. And I remember thinking, "Okay, I've done this before, I can do it again, it's just a temporary crunch until we hire replacements." But the replacements took forever to find, and then they had to be trained, and... well, it just never really let up. 

And that's when I noticed it starting. At first, I thought I was just burning the candle at both ends, you know? Just the stress of the transition. I figured once the new hires were up to speed, I'd bounce back. But the new hires *are* up to speed now. They've been fully integrated for over a year. The workload is manageable again. I'm not working sixty-hour weeks anymore. But that feeling... that absolute drain, that grayness... it never left. It just moved in right around that two-year, four-month mark, when I was back in the thick of operations, and it unpacked its bags and stayed. So, yeah, it's been a long stretch of just... feeling like a battery that won't hold a charge, day in and day out, for well over two years now.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in or look forward to?

Well, you know, like I was saying just a few minutes ago, it really is a struggle to find anything that gives me that old spark. I mean, I really have racked my brain, and I've tried—believe me, my wife and I have both tried to find just one thing that I can genuinely say I look forward to. But it all just comes back to what I was telling you before. For a long time now, there’s just been this... this pervasive gray, flat feeling hanging over me most days. It's like a fog that just won't lift, no matter what I'm doing or who I'm with. 

I mentioned the fishing down at the lake, and tending to the tomatoes—the Big Boys and the heirlooms I planted—and even those Sunday evening church concerts. Those were my lifelines, you know? The things that kept me going through the stress of the work week. And now... well, I know I already said this, but it really is the best way I can describe it: they just feel like items on a checklist instead of something I actually enjoy. 

It's so frustrating because I'll wake up on a Saturday, and I'll think, "Okay, today is the day. Today I'm going to take the boat out, and I'm going to feel that old excitement when the sun comes up over the water." And I'll get all the gear loaded up in the truck—the tackle box, the rods, the cooler, making sure I have the right lures for the weather—and I drive down there, and I'm just... going through the motions. Unload the boat. Check. Bait the hook. Check. Cast the line. Check. 

There's no joy in it. And it's not just the big hobbies, either. It's everything. It's sitting on the porch with my morning coffee. It's watching a football game on Sunday afternoon. I used to love doing those things, but now it's just... flat. Just a gray wash over everything. I keep waiting for something, anything, to break through it, to make me feel that little jolt of happiness or anticipation, but... no. Honestly, doctor, no. I can't think of a single thing right now that I truly look forward to or find any real pleasure in doing anymore. It's all just part of the routine now, just another box to tick off before the day is done.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight recently?

Weight? Well... yeah, I suppose I have, actually. It’s funny you ask that, because I wasn't really paying attention to the scale or anything. I mean, I'm certainly not on a diet, and I haven't been trying to lose weight at all—at my age, I'm not exactly trying to trim down for a marathon or anything, you know? But... well, my appetite has just been off more days than not lately. 

It’s like my stomach just forgets to tell my brain that it’s time to eat. I'll be sitting at my desk at work, looking at network logs or dealing with vendor emails—because even though the new hires are handling the daily fires like I mentioned, there's always some vendor trying to push a software update that we have to review—and I'll just completely work right through lunch. I won't even notice the time passing. It’ll be two or three in the afternoon, and my assistant will ask if I want anything from the cafeteria, and I'll realize I haven't had a single bite all day. And the strange thing is, I don't even care. I just wave her off.

And then I get home, and... well, like I was saying earlier about that pot roast my wife made. I just sit there and pick at my dinner. She’ll make a really nice meal, and I just push the food around the plate. I’ll take a few bites so she doesn't worry too much, but I just don't have the drive to finish it. It all just tastes like cardboard anyway. 

Because of all that, my wife actually pointed out just the other day that my clothes aren't fitting right. She was folding laundry and she mentioned that my pants are looking awfully baggy on me. And she's right, I put on my work slacks the other morning—the navy blue ones I usually wear on Thursdays—and I had to pull my belt an extra notch tighter just to keep them from sliding down. They're definitely a lot looser. So, yes, I am losing weight, but it’s purely by accident, just because eating feels like... well, just another chore I don't have the interest for.
Do you find yourself moving or speaking more slowly than you used to?

Moving or speaking more slowly? Well... no, I don't think so. It's an interesting question, because like I was saying earlier, I definitely *feel* like I'm wading through molasses on the inside, just completely drained of that old energy, but outwardly? Physically? I'm pretty sure I'm still moving at my regular pace. 

I mean, just this past Wednesday—or was it Tuesday? No, it was Wednesday, because the building management was doing their monthly fire alarm testing—I had to get from my office on the third floor all the way down to the basement server room. One of the new hires, a nice kid but still getting his bearings with our specific setup, couldn't locate the primary routing switch for the east wing. I had to physically go down there and point it out to him. I walked down those three flights of stairs and down that long concrete hallway just as briskly as I would have five or ten years ago. My knees creaked a little bit, sure, but that's just the reality of being sixty-three, not... not moving in slow motion or anything like that. 

And as for speaking, well, my wife would probably be the first to tell you that I haven't lost my ability to talk at my normal speed. I still run the morning stand-up meetings with the IT department every Tuesday and Thursday at 8:30 AM sharp. We have a very tight agenda in those meetings—we have to go over the unresolved ticket queue, check the overnight backup logs, make sure the security patches from the night before actually deployed to all the workstations correctly—and if I were talking any slower than usual, we'd never get out of that conference room before 10 AM. I have to keep the pace up just to keep everyone else on track and get them back to their desks. 

So, no, I really haven't noticed any changes like that. My team hasn't been asking me to repeat myself, and nobody is telling me to hurry up when I'm walking down the hall. It’s really just that internal feeling of exhaustion, that heavy grayness I was talking about, rather than my actual physical body slowing down. I might feel like a battery that won't hold a charge, but the motor is still running at the exact same RPM it always has, if that makes sense.
Do you often feel worthless or have a low opinion of yourself?

Worthless? Well... no. No, I really don't think so. I mean, it's a fair question, considering how drained I've been feeling, but honestly, my opinion of myself is still pretty solid. I know exactly what I bring to the table. 

Take my job, for instance. I've been in information systems management for... gosh, it has to be going on thirty-five years now. I started back when we were still dealing with token-ring networks and green-screen terminals, you know? So I've built up a lot of expertise over the decades, and I know my value there. Just last month, actually, we had this massive headache with a database migration. The external vendor promised a completely seamless transition, but of course, right at 4:00 PM on a Friday, the whole primary server locked up. The new hires were practically hyperventilating, pulling up all these internet forums and trying to run all these complex diagnostic scripts that were just making things worse. But I just walked in, told everyone to take a breath, and traced the issue back to a simple misconfigured subnet mask that the vendor's automated tool had completely botched. I had us back online in under an hour. 

So, when I look at things like that, I know I'm highly competent. I know I'm valuable to the company, and I know I've always been a good provider for my wife. We paid off the mortgage on the house three years ago, we've got a decent retirement fund building up... I've done well for us. I don't sit around beating myself up or thinking I'm a failure or a burden or anything like that. The track record is there, plain as day. 

It really all just goes back to what I was saying before about that... that flat, gray feeling. I know I'm a capable guy, and I know I have a lot of worth, but I just don't have the drive to care about it right now. It's like having a top-of-the-line sports car sitting in the driveway, but the gas tank is completely empty. You know the car is valuable, you know it's a great machine, but it's just not going anywhere. So, no, I don't feel worthless at all. I just feel... tired of running the engine, I suppose.
Have you noticed any changes in your interest in sex recently?

Interest in sex? Well... no. No, I wouldn't say so. It's actually one of the few things that seems completely untouched by all this... this grayness I've been describing to you. 

My wife and I, we've been married a long time—thirty-four years this coming May, actually. We met back when I was just taking a few college courses, right before I got hired at my first real tech job, back when data processing meant literal punch cards and magnetic tape. Anyway, at sixty-three, you naturally settle into a comfortable rhythm with your partner, you know? It’s not like we’re swinging from the chandeliers like kids in their twenties, but the desire, the interest... it’s still exactly where it’s been for the last decade or so. 

We have our routine. Usually, Friday nights are our time to really reconnect after the week. I'll finally put my phone on silent so the junior admins can't page me about some minor server hiccup or a forgotten password, and we'll just have a nice evening to ourselves. And the intimacy is still very much there. I still find her just as attractive as I always have, and I still have the drive for that physical connection. 

It's strange, really, when you think about it. I can sit at the dinner table and not care at all about a beautiful pot roast, like I mentioned earlier, and I can feel totally wiped out just sitting at my desk looking at emails, but when it comes to my wife and our private life? The engine still fires up just fine. It's like that part of my brain is walled off from the exhaustion. So, no, I haven't noticed any drop-off or changes in my sex drive at all. It's just steady, same as always.
Have you ever thought about ending your life or had any thoughts of suicide?

Ending my life? Oh... no. No, absolutely not. I can see why you'd ask, given how much I've been going on about feeling like I'm wading through molasses and just... just being so drained all the time, but no, it's never crossed my mind to do anything like that. 

I mean, I'm a very practical guy. Always have been. You kind of have to be in my line of work, dealing with systems and infrastructure all day—you're always looking to keep things running, not pull the plug entirely. And I've got too much here that I'm responsible for. I mentioned my wife earlier, and... well, I could never do something like that to her. We've built this whole life together over the last thirty-four years, paid off the house, got our routines... I'm not going to just abandon ship. 

Actually, it's funny, just this morning before I drove over here for this appointment, I was standing in the driveway with my coffee, looking up at the roof. The gutters on the east side of the house are already starting to get a little backed up, and the autumn leaves haven't even really started coming down heavy yet. We have these two big oak trees near the property line that just dump leaves everywhere come late October. Anyway, I was standing there, mentally mapping out which weekend I'm going to get the extension ladder out of the garage and clear them all out before the first big freeze. I've got a whole system for it with the hose and this attachment I rigged up. I think... well, I'm pretty sure a guy who's thinking about ending it all doesn't stand in his driveway at seven in the morning worrying about water damage to his siding, right? 

So, no. It's really just this... this fatigue. This grayness. I might be tired of the daily grind, and I really wish I could get my old energy back, but I definitely want to be here. I'm not looking to check out early. I just want the engine to feel like it's running right again, you know?
Have you experienced any changes in your sleep patterns?

Sleep? Well... yeah, actually. That's one area where things have definitely been a bit off lately. It’s incredibly frustrating, to be honest with you. 

Going to sleep isn't the issue at all. My wife and I usually head up to bed around ten-thirty, right after the local news—she likes to catch the weather forecast for her gardening—and I usually fall asleep all right. I'm usually out like a light the second my head hits the pillow. But then... well, it's almost like clockwork. Right around four in the morning, my eyes just pop open. 4:12, 4:17, somewhere right in that exact window. 

And it's not a slow, groggy wake-up, either. It's like my brain just instantly boots up, like a system coming back online after a hard reset. Before I even fully register that I'm awake, my mind is already racing, just automatically sorting through all these work problems. I'll be lying there in the pitch black, staring at the ceiling fan, thinking about server redundancies, or I'll start stressing over these new data compliance deadlines we have coming up for Q3. We have this massive security audit looming, and for some reason, my brain just decides 4:00 AM is the perfect time to run through firewall configurations and user access protocols. 

Once that starts, that's it. The sleep cycle is completely broken. I don't want to toss and turn and wake my wife, because she's a terribly light sleeper, so I just... I just lie there. For two whole hours. I try to force myself back to sleep, I try that deep breathing stuff, but the gears are already turning way too fast. So I just lie there in the dark until the alarm finally goes off at six. 

By the time I actually get up to go downstairs and start the coffee maker, I'm already exhausted. It just leaves me feeling like the night didn't really count, you know? Like I didn't actually get any real rest, I just laid horizontally for a few hours while my brain worked the night shift. So, yeah, the sleep situation hasn't been great at all.
Have you noticed yourself fidgeting or feeling restless more often than usual?

Restless? Fidgeting? No, not really. I mean, I'm not bouncing my leg under the desk or pacing around the server room or anything like that. If anything, it's the exact opposite, like I was saying before with this... this heaviness. 

I'm sitting at my desk for eight, sometimes nine hours a day, depending on what kind of fires we're putting out. And my desk setup, it's actually pretty ergonomic. I made sure of that when we transitioned to this hybrid work model a couple of years ago. I got one of those Herman Miller chairs—the Aeron, you know the one with the mesh back? It really supports the lumbar region, which is crucial when you're my age and staring at dual monitors all day. I even have a standing desk converter, one of the motorized ones where you just push a button and it glides up. But honestly? I haven't pushed that button in months. 

I just sit there. I don't feel the urge to get up and move around, I don't feel jittery. The junior guys, the ones fresh out of their computer science programs, they're always up and down, grabbing another energy drink, tossing a stress ball around, tapping their pens during stand-up meetings. I watch them and I just think, where do you get the energy? I'm perfectly content—well, maybe content isn't the right word, but I'm perfectly stationary. I just sit there, feeling like I'm made of lead, trying to get through the inbox. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm restless at all. My body just wants to stay put.
Have you experienced a significantly depressed mood for most of the day, nearly every day?

Depressed? I suppose... well, maybe. I don't know if I'd use the word depressed, like I'm sitting around crying or anything, because I'm definitely not. It's really more of this... this gray, flat feeling. And it's been like that for a long, long time now, pretty much most days. It’s hard to explain to someone who hasn't felt it, but it’s like the color is just completely washed out of my routine. 

Take my weekends, for example. I used to really look forward to things. Like tending the tomatoes. We have these three raised cedar beds out back—I built them myself a few years ago because my knees were getting a little stiff bending down in the dirt—and I always took a lot of pride in them. I'd spend hours getting the soil pH just right, tying the vines to the stakes, pruning the suckers. But lately? I go out there with the hose and it just feels like a chore. 

Or fishing. I've got this little 14-foot aluminum boat I take out to the reservoir. Used to be my absolute favorite way to spend a Saturday, just me and a thermos of coffee out on the water, seeing what's biting. Now, the thought of hooking up the trailer, checking the outboard motor, packing the tackle box... I just don't have the desire. 

Even stuff with my wife, like... well, a couple weeks ago we went to this church concert. The choir was doing a whole special evening program, and usually I really enjoy that sort of thing. I like the acoustics in our sanctuary, and they always have a great brass section. But I just sat there in the pew, looking at the bulletin, just waiting for the hour to be up. It’s like everything—the fishing, the tomatoes, the concerts—they all just feel like items on a checklist now instead of something I actually enjoy doing. You know how it is at work, you just go down the list, crossing things off so you can say they're done and move on to the next ticket? That's what my whole life feels like right now. Just a long checklist, day after day of this flat, gray feeling.
Can you think of anything that brings you a sense of pleasure or enjoyment?

Pleasure? Enjoyment? Honestly... no. I really can't think of anything. And I've tried, I really have. It's not like I haven't been actively trying to find something that sparks a little bit of... of anything, really. 

Like I was saying about the fishing, right? Last month, I thought, maybe I just need new gear. Sometimes that helps, you know? A new piece of tech or equipment can kind of reboot your interest. So I went down to the Bass Pro Shop out on Route 9. Huge place, you could get lost in there for hours. I spent a good forty-five minutes just looking at different crankbaits and spinnerbaits, comparing the weights and the colors. I even bought this new medium-action spinning rod, carbon fiber, really lightweight, nice cork handle. I thought, 'Okay, this is going to be great. I'll take this out on Saturday, it'll be just like old times.' 

But then Saturday rolled around, and... nothing. I looked at the new rod sitting there in the corner of the garage, right next to the snowblower, and I just felt absolutely nothing. No excitement, no anticipation. I didn't even take the tags off it. It's just sitting there collecting dust now. 

And it's the same with the food, too. My wife, she’s a wonderful cook, truly. She makes this incredible pot roast—slow cooks it all day with carrots, pearl onions, these little red potatoes, a really rich beef broth with just a splash of red wine. It used to be my absolute favorite meal. When I’d pull into the driveway after work and smell that coming from the kitchen vent, my mouth would literally start watering. But she made it last Sunday, and I sat down at the table, took a bite, and it was just... food. It was just fuel. I chewed it, I swallowed it, but there was no joy in it. I couldn't even appreciate the tenderness of the meat or the seasoning. I just ate it because it was 6:00 PM and that's when we eat dinner. 

So, to answer your question... no. Whether it's my hobbies, my favorite meals, spending time with my wife... it all just feels incredibly flat. I can't remember the last time I actually felt a genuine sense of pleasure from anything at all. It's just... it's all just gray.
Have you had a period of at least two weeks where you felt depressed or lost interest in most activities nearly every day?

Two weeks? Oh... well, yes. Definitely. I mean, two weeks would be a drop in the bucket at this point. If I really sit back and look at the calendar, trying to pinpoint when this whole gray, flat feeling really settled in and just... parked itself over me... it’s been much, much longer than that. 

This has been going on since I was pulled back into full operational leadership, which was about two years and four months ago. I remember the timeline exactly because we were right in the middle of our Q3 fiscal planning. We had this younger guy, a really bright kid we'd hired to take over the day-to-day operations so I could transition into more of a high-level strategic role. I was supposed to be looking at the big picture, you know, five-year technology roadmaps, that sort of thing. But he ended up jumping ship for some startup down in Austin. Left us completely in the lurch right in the middle of a massive cloud migration project. 

So, the VP comes to me and says, "We need you back in the trenches, just temporarily, until we backfill the position." But you know how "temporary" goes in corporate IT, right? The hiring freeze came down a month later, and suddenly I'm back to managing all the tier-three escalations, negotiating vendor contracts, sitting in endless operational stand-ups every single morning. 

And that is exactly when this whole... this total loss of interest started. Two years and four months ago. It wasn't like a switch flipped overnight, but it just sort of drained out of me week by week once I was back in that operational seat. And it hasn't let up since. Every single day for over two years, just waking up, logging on, putting out the fires, and feeling absolutely nothing about any of it. Not the work, not the fishing, not the garden. Just that long checklist I mentioned. So, yes, it's been well over two weeks.
Have you experienced any psychomotor agitation or retardation nearly every day?

Psychomotor... agitation? Or retardation? I'm not entirely sure I know exactly what you mean by that in a medical sense, but if you're asking if I'm pacing around the room bouncing off the walls, or on the flip side, moving like I'm walking through wet cement... no, I haven't noticed anything like that. 

I mean, if you think about it, I sit at a desk for nine, sometimes ten hours a day managing these IT systems, so I don't do a whole lot of moving to begin with. I've got this whole ergonomic setup at the home office—a Herman Miller Aeron chair, dual 27-inch monitors, one of those expensive standing desk converters that, to be perfectly honest with you, I haven't actually raised to the standing position since maybe last November. But as far as my actual physical movements go? No, I wouldn't say I'm restless. I'm not fidgeting with my pen or bouncing my leg during my Monday morning vendor calls or anything. I just sit there and look at the screen. 

And I don't think I'm moving or talking any slower than I usually do, either. My wife hasn't said anything about it, and believe me, she's usually the very first person to point out if I'm doing something out of the ordinary, like tapping my foot or sighing too much or whatever. My knees get a little stiff, sure, like I mentioned with the cedar garden beds earlier, but that's just a bit of arthritis, you know? That's just what happens when you're sixty-three. 

So, no, physically, my body is just doing what it always does, at the exact same speed it always has. It's really just that internal feeling I was talking about before, that total flatness, not my physical movements. Everything on the outside is functioning at the normal pace.
Are there any activities that you find pleasure in or enjoy doing?

Well, I know I kind of touched on this a few minutes ago when we were talking about the fishing gear and my wife's pot roast, but... honestly, no. It’s exactly like I was saying. For a really long time now, there’s just been this... this completely gray, flat feeling most days. It's like a heavy blanket that just sits over everything, and it bleeds into absolutely every corner of my life. 

Even the things I really used to look forward to, they just don't register anymore. Take the garden, for example. I mentioned my knees getting a bit stiff around those cedar garden beds earlier. I used to absolutely love tending the tomatoes out there. I'd grow these big heirloom varieties—Cherokee Purples, Brandywines, Early Girls—and I'd be out there every single evening after work. I'd check the soil moisture, pinch off the suckers, tie the vines to the stakes... I used to really look forward to it. It was peaceful, you know? A really tactile way to decompress after staring at spreadsheets and server metrics for ten hours. But now? I just go out there with the hose because if I don't, the plants will die. It feels exactly like an item on a checklist. "Water tomatoes." Check. There's no satisfaction in it whatsoever. 

And it’s the exact same story with social things. My wife and I, we usually go to these church concerts. The choir puts on a really nice program a few times a year, and they'll bring in some guest musicians, maybe a brass section or a string quartet. We went to one recently, and usually, I'd really enjoy the music. The acoustics in our sanctuary are actually fantastic, really high vaulted ceilings. But I just sat there in the pew, holding the paper program, and I found myself just counting how many songs were left until we could get back in the car and go home. It wasn't something I enjoyed even a little bit. It was just another box to check off for the evening.

We have these three raised cedar beds out back—I built them myself a few years ago because my knees were getting a little stiff bending down in the dirt—and I always took a lot of pride in them. I'd spend hours getting the soil pH just right, tying the vines to the stakes, pruning the suckers. But lately? I go out there with the hose and it just feels like a chore. 

Or fishing. I've got this little 14-foot aluminum boat I take out to the reservoir. Used to be my absolute favorite way to spend a Saturday, just me and a thermos of coffee out on the water, seeing what's biting. Now, the thought of hooking up the trailer, checking the outboard motor, packing the tackle box... I just don't have the desire. 

Even stuff with my wife, like... well, a couple weeks ago we went to this church concert. The choir was doing a whole special evening program, and usually I really enjoy that sort of thing. I like the acoustics in our sanctuary, and they always have a great brass section. But I just sat there in the pew, looking at the bulletin, just waiting for the hour to be up. It’s like everything—the fishing, the tomatoes, the concerts—they all just feel like items on a checklist now instead of something I actually enjoy doing. You know how it is at work, you just go down the list, crossing things off so you can say they're done and move on to the next ticket? That's what my whole life feels like right now. Just a long checklist, day after day of this flat, gray feeling.

doctor.question: Can you think of anything that brings you a sense of pleasure or enjoyment?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about anhedonia (loss of interest or pleasure), which is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Pleasure? Enjoyment? Honestly... no. I really can't think of anything. And I've tried, I really have. It's not like I haven't been actively trying to find something that sparks a little bit of... of anything, really. 

Like I was saying about the fishing, right? Last month, I thought, maybe I just need new gear. Sometimes that helps, you know? A new piece of tech or equipment can kind of reboot your interest. So I went down to the Bass Pro Shop out on Route 9. Huge place, you could get lost in there for hours. I spent a good forty-five minutes just looking at different crankbaits and spinnerbaits, comparing the weights and the colors. I even bought this new medium-action spinning rod, carbon fiber, really lightweight, nice cork handle. I thought, 'Okay, this is going to be great. I'll take this out on Saturday, it'll be just like old times.' 

But then Saturday rolled around, and... nothing. I looked at the new rod sitting there in the corner of the garage, right next to the snowblower, and I just felt absolutely nothing. No excitement, no anticipation. I didn't even take the tags off it. It's just sitting there collecting dust now. 

And it's the same with the food, too. My wife, she’s a wonderful cook, truly. She makes this incredible pot roast—slow cooks it all day with carrots, pearl onions, these little red potatoes, a really rich beef broth with just a splash of red wine. It used to be my absolute favorite meal. When I’d pull into the driveway after work and smell that coming from the kitchen vent, my mouth would literally start watering. But she made it last Sunday, and I sat down at the table, took a bite, and it was just... food. It was just fuel. I chewed it, I swallowed it, but there was no joy in it. I couldn't even appreciate the tenderness of the meat or the seasoning. I just ate it because it was 6:00 PM and that's when we eat dinner. 

So, to answer your question... no. Whether it's my hobbies, my favorite meals, spending time with my wife... it all just feels incredibly flat. I can't remember the last time I actually felt a genuine sense of pleasure from anything at all. It's just... it's all just gray.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition meets the criteria for a major depressive episode
doctor.question: Have you had a period of at least two weeks where you felt depressed or lost interest in most activities nearly every day?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since I was pulled back into full operational leadership, about two years and four months ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the depressed mood or loss of interest has lasted for a specific timeframe (at least two weeks), which directly relates to the duration of my symptoms.

patient.answer:
Two weeks? Oh... well, yes. Definitely. I mean, two weeks would be a drop in the bucket at this point. If I really sit back and look at the calendar, trying to pinpoint when this whole gray, flat feeling really settled in and just... parked itself over me... it’s been much, much longer than that. 

This has been going on since I was pulled back into full operational leadership, which was about two years and four months ago. I remember the timeline exactly because we were right in the middle of our Q3 fiscal planning. We had this younger guy, a really bright kid we'd hired to take over the day-to-day operations so I could transition into more of a high-level strategic role. I was supposed to be looking at the big picture, you know, five-year technology roadmaps, that sort of thing. But he ended up jumping ship for some startup down in Austin. Left us completely in the lurch right in the middle of a massive cloud migration project. 

So, the VP comes to me and says, "We need you back in the trenches, just temporarily, until we backfill the position." But you know how "temporary" goes in corporate IT, right? The hiring freeze came down a month later, and suddenly I'm back to managing all the tier-three escalations, negotiating vendor contracts, sitting in endless operational stand-ups every single morning. 

And that is exactly when this whole... this total loss of interest started. Two years and four months ago. It wasn't like a switch flipped overnight, but it just sort of drained out of me week by week once I was back in that operational seat. And it hasn't let up since. Every single day for over two years, just waking up, logging on, putting out the fires, and feeling absolutely nothing about any of it. Not the work, not the fishing, not the garden. Just that long checklist I mentioned. So, yes, it's been well over two weeks.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of the patient's depression to differentiate between F32.0 and F32.1
doctor.question: Have you experienced any psychomotor agitation or retardation nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor agitation or retardation, which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Psychomotor... agitation? Or retardation? I'm not entirely sure I know exactly what you mean by that in a medical sense, but if you're asking if I'm pacing around the room bouncing off the walls, or on the flip side, moving like I'm walking through wet cement... no, I haven't noticed anything like that. 

I mean, if you think about it, I sit at a desk for nine, sometimes ten hours a day managing these IT systems, so I don't do a whole lot of moving to begin with. I've got this whole ergonomic setup at the home office—a Herman Miller Aeron chair, dual 27-inch monitors, one of those expensive standing desk converters that, to be perfectly honest with you, I haven't actually raised to the standing position since maybe last November. But as far as my actual physical movements go? No, I wouldn't say I'm restless. I'm not fidgeting with my pen or bouncing my leg during my Monday morning vendor calls or anything. I just sit there and look at the screen. 

And I don't think I'm moving or talking any slower than I usually do, either. My wife hasn't said anything about it, and believe me, she's usually the very first person to point out if I'm doing something out of the ordinary, like tapping my foot or sighing too much or whatever. My knees get a little stiff, sure, like I mentioned with the cedar garden beds earlier, but that's just a bit of arthritis, you know? That's just what happens when you're sixty-three. 

So, no, physically, my body is just doing what it always does, at the exact same speed it always has. It's really just that internal feeling I was talking about before, that total flatness, not my physical movements. Everything on the outside is functioning at the normal pace.

doctor.question: Are there any activities that you find pleasure in or enjoy doing?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: For a long time now there’s been this gray, flat feeling most days, where even things I used to look forward to like fishing, tending the tomatoes, or a church concert feel like items on a checklist instead of something I enjoy.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about loss of pleasure or enjoyment (anhedonia), which is covered by the manifestation of Depressed Mood where the patient describes a gray, flat feeling and a lack of enjoyment in previously favored activities like fishing and gardening.

patient.answer:
Well, I know I kind of touched on this a few minutes ago when we were talking about the fishing gear and my wife's pot roast, but... honestly, no. It’s exactly like I was saying. For a really long time now, there’s just been this... this completely gray, flat feeling most days. It's like a heavy blanket that just sits over everything, and it bleeds into absolutely every corner of my life. 

Even the things I really used to look forward to, they just don't register anymore. Take the garden, for example. I mentioned my knees getting a bit stiff around those cedar garden beds earlier. I used to absolutely love tending the tomatoes out there. I'd grow these big heirloom varieties—Cherokee Purples, Brandywines, Early Girls—and I'd be out there every single evening after work. I'd check the soil moisture, pinch off the suckers, tie the vines to the stakes... I used to really look forward to it. It was peaceful, you know? A really tactile way to decompress after staring at spreadsheets and server metrics for ten hours. But now? I just go out there with the hose because if I don't, the plants will die. It feels exactly like an item on a checklist. "Water tomatoes." Check. There's no satisfaction in it whatsoever. 

And it’s the exact same story with social things. My wife and I, we usually go to these church concerts. The choir puts on a really nice program a few times a year, and they'll bring in some guest musicians, maybe a brass section or a string quartet. We went to one recently, and usually, I'd really enjoy the music. The acoustics in our sanctuary are actually fantastic, really high vaulted ceilings. But I just sat there in the pew, holding the paper program, and I found myself just counting how many songs were left until we could get back in the car and go home. It wasn't something I enjoyed even a little bit. It was just another box to check off for the evening. 

So, yeah, whether it's the fishing, tending to the tomatoes, or sitting through a church concert... none of it brings me any pleasure. It all just feels like a long, exhausting checklist instead of something I actually enjoy doing. That gray feeling just kind of washes the color out of all of it.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, like I was mentioning right at the start of our conversation... I know we already touched on the timeline a bit, but two weeks is really just a fraction of it. This has been going on since I was pulled back into full operational leadership, about two years and four months ago. 

And as far as a letup goes? No, absolutely none. You know, you always hope that maybe taking a few days off will hit the reset button. Like last year, I took some PTO, which is nearly impossible to do when you are managing the day-to-day IT operations and dealing with all those escalations I mentioned, but I managed to get away for a long weekend. I thought, okay, I will get away from the dual monitors, get away from the endless vendor emails, and maybe this heavy, tired feeling will finally lift. But it was exactly the same. I just sat around feeling just as flat and exhausted on my time off as I do on the clock. So it has been two years and four months, day in and day out, without any sort of break or relief from it whatsoever. Not even for a single afternoon.
